section_summary: This section centers on U.S. export policy toward Japan, including proposals for wider embargoes, licensing rules for petroleum and strategic materials, and reports of continuing shipments of gasoline, lubricants, steel, rails, fluorspar, and other commodities. It contains internal State Department analyses, diplomatic and consular reports, correspondence from members of Congress and private citizens, and replies explaining the Export Control Act and existing restrictions. The section also addresses aid to China, Pacific security, Australian controls on scrap exports, and concern that supplies sent to Japan or the Soviet Union might support the Axis powers.

subfiles.title: Continuation of Harry B. Price's analysis of American newspaper editorials on Far Eastern policy
subfiles.about: Tabulates editorial positions on the Burma Road, embargoes against Japan, Pacific cooperation, bases, relations with Russia, and resistance to Japanese expansion.
subfiles.summary: The continuation presents numerical counts of editorials supporting, opposing, or merely discussing several possible U.S. policies in Asia. It shows especially strong editorial support for embargoes on war materials and active resistance to further Japanese expansion, while also recording isolationist and Europe-first positions.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledgment of Price's editorial survey
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Price's January 2 analysis of editorials in 233 newspapers from 38 states.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks Price for the detailed and interesting survey. He states that he is circulating the letter among his associates for their information.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese demand for unrestricted motor lubricating oil
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese request to Standard-Vacuum Oil Company for any available quantity of motor lubricating oil.
subfiles.summary: Walden advised that Japanese buyers sought motor lubricating oil for delivery during January through March 1941. Although not classified as an aviation lubricant, the product could be used in aircraft and was available in large quantities only from the United States; because it was not prohibited, the company intended to continue selling it.

subfiles.title: Legation despatch on proposed Costa Rican rails-for-locomotives exchange with Japan
subfiles.about: Reports a proposal to send discarded Costa Rican rails to Japan in exchange for two locomotives and seeks help finding a U.S. purchaser.
subfiles.summary: Most of the despatch is illegible in the OCR, but the surrounding text identifies it as Despatch No. 2853 concerning two or three thousand tons of discarded rails. The Legation suggested referring the question to the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce and possibly the National Defense Council so that the rails might instead be sold in the United States.

subfiles.title: Internal memorandum on Costa Rican rails and locomotives
subfiles.about: Requests advice on whether the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce could help find a U.S. purchaser for Costa Rican rails otherwise intended for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes the Legation's inquiry about exchanging two or three thousand tons of discarded rails for two locomotives from Japan. It suggests that selling the rails in the United States might provide funds to buy the locomotives already available in Costa Rica and asks whether the Commerce Bureau could act.
keywords: Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce

subfiles.title: Instruction to San José concerning proposed shipment of rails to Japan
subfiles.about: Replies to the Legation's inquiry about the proposed rails-for-locomotives transaction.
subfiles.summary: The poorly preserved instruction refers to the Legation's inquiry and states that the matter had been referred informally to the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce. It also directs that further inquiry be made concerning the intentions behind the proposed transaction.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japan Gasoline Company's dispute with Universal Oil Products
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Assesses a Japanese Embassy proposal for resolving litigation over Universal Oil Products contracts.
subfiles.summary: Morito Morishima pressed for consideration of an Embassy proposal concerning the Japan Gasoline Company's suit against Universal Oil Products. Green noted that the proposed compromise might require Universal to disclose processes involving toluene and synthetic rubber that it did not wish to give Japanese interests, and he recommended making no further response unless instructed.

subfiles.title: Senator George's request for information concerning Senator Holman's export complaint
subfiles.about: Forwards Senator Rufus C. Holman's letter and requests information for a reply.
subfiles.summary: George transmits Holman's inquiry about reported exports through Portland to the Soviet Union and possibly Japan. He asks the State Department for information on which he may base an answer.

subfiles.title: Senator Holman letter on reported Portland shipments to Russia and Japan
subfiles.about: Reports alleged shipments of airplane beacons, copper, steel, and iron through Portland to Vladivostok and possibly Japan.
subfiles.summary: Holman quotes his sister's account, based on observations by Huntington Malarkey and John Burgard, of unusual freight moving through Portland. He asks George to verify the report and comment on the wisdom of exporting such materials to the Soviet Union, while protecting his sister's identity.

subfiles.title: Draft State Department reply to Senator George on exports to the Soviet Union
subfiles.about: Explains U.S. export-licensing policy in response to Holman's allegations about shipments to the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: The reply says that the Department cannot confirm the destination of the specific shipments but notes that no general embargo applies to exports to the Soviet Union. It outlines controls under the Act of July 2, 1940, explains that aviation gasoline and scrap iron are barred outside the British Empire and Western Hemisphere, and encloses the relevant proclamations, executive orders, regulations, and releases.

subfiles.title: Should We Impose Embargoes on Japan?
subfiles.from: W. R. Peck, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Argues for a gradual expansion of U.S. export and import embargoes against Japan.
subfiles.summary: The paper links trade with Japan to the wars in Europe and China and reviews U.S. efforts to aid China while maintaining normal relations with Japan. It assesses the risks that stronger economic pressure might provoke war, a Japanese seizure of the Netherlands East Indies, or attacks on Hong Kong or Singapore, but judges those outcomes unlikely in the near term. It concludes that cautiously expanded embargoes would exploit Japan's dependence on foreign supplies, weaken an Axis partner, protect American interests, and improve China's prospects.

subfiles.title: Treasury transmittal of E. D. McMahon's strategic-minerals proposal
subfiles.about: Forwards McMahon's proposal for keeping Mexican strategic metals away from Japan and Germany.
subfiles.summary: The Treasury sends the State Department a copy of McMahon's jointly addressed letter. It also encloses a copy of the Treasury's reply to him.

subfiles.title: Treasury acknowledgment to E. D. McMahon
subfiles.about: Acknowledges McMahon's proposal concerning strategic commodities.
subfiles.summary: The badly degraded copy thanks McMahon for his interest in the issue. It indicates that the matter was receiving attention and refers to Secretary Hull or the State Department's interest.

subfiles.title: Suggested Plan for Keeping Mexican Mercury, Tungsten, Molybdenum, and Vanadium Away from Japan and Germany
subfiles.to: Henry Morgenthau Jr.; William S. Knudsen; Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Proposes tying U.S. purchases of Mexican silver to purchases of strategic minerals so those materials cannot reach Japan or Germany.
subfiles.summary: McMahon recommends refusing to buy Mexican silver alone and instead requiring Mexico to sell mercury, tungsten, molybdenum, and vanadium in a combined arrangement. He advocates economic pressure under the Good Neighbor policy, prefers commodity purchases to loans, and suggests adapting the system to countries such as Brazil.

subfiles.title: Consular report on fluorspar shipments from Manzanillo to Japan
subfiles.from: Henry A. Hoyt, American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese contracts for monthly fluorspar shipments from Manzanillo and lists scheduled vessels and cargoes.
subfiles.summary: Hoyt reports that Japanese shipping lines contracted to load 5,000 tons of fluorspar monthly beginning in March 1941, with the mineral originating in Guerrero. He lists five planned shipments and adds that, although no specific mercury contracts were known, large quantities of mercury continued to leave the port.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Grew telegram on Japanese supply shortages and press criticism
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram reporting Japanese difficulty obtaining machine tools and high-octane gasoline and press criticism of exports to Russia.
subfiles.summary: The sheet summarizes a Japanese press editorial attacking the lifting of the moral embargo on exports to Russia that were allegedly reaching Germany. It directs researchers to Grew's Telegram No. 144 in another file classification.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Richard G. Casey on Australian export controls and aid to China
subfiles.about: Records a conversation with the Australian Minister about Australia's steel and scrap embargo, naval cooperation, and U.S. measures supporting China and the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: Casey supplied a statement announcing Australia's embargo on steel and scrap exports to Japan and discussed recent naval conferences. When he asked about sending U.S. naval vessels to Australia or Singapore, Hull cited the Chinese loan, reinforcement of the Philippines, and prospective U.S. controls on finished iron and steel before deferring further consideration.

subfiles.title: Australian Exports of Scrap Iron and Steel
subfiles.about: States that Australia prohibited steel and scrap-iron exports outside the British Empire beginning November 27, 1940.
subfiles.summary: The statement explains that the embargo was imposed to conserve supplies for national and imperial requirements. It notes that Australia exported A£240,000 worth of iron and steel scrap to Japan during the 1939–40 financial year; the file contains three copies.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Casey conversation memorandum to London
subfiles.about: Sends the London Embassy a confidential copy of the December 3 conversation memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses the memorandum concerning Australia's embargo on steel and scrap-iron exports and U.S. aid to China. The copy is provided confidentially for the Embassy's information and files.

subfiles.title: Congressman Thomas forwards Rolland Bradley's gasoline complaint
subfiles.about: Forwards a Houston committee's letter about gasoline shipments to Japan and asks the Department to reply directly.
subfiles.summary: Thomas sends Rolland Bradley's letter to the State Department and asks for the Department's reaction to its claims. He requests that the original be returned after it has served its purpose.

subfiles.title: Houston committee complaint about gasoline exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Rolland Bradley and Robert J. Peden
subfiles.about: Urges action against monthly shipments of lower-octane gasoline from Houston and other Texas ports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The committee alleges that approximately 100,000 barrels of gasoline per month were going to Japan and could easily be chemically treated for military use. Bradley and Peden argue that the trade undermined the Open Door policy, aided Japanese aggression in China, raised U.S. prices, and might eventually supply weapons used against American forces.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Rolland Bradley on gasoline shipments
subfiles.from: Leonard H. Price for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that no general embargo covered Japan but that strategic exports were controlled through licensing.
subfiles.summary: The Department says it cannot confirm Bradley's particular shipments without additional details and acknowledges that some material may have been bound for Japan. It explains that aviation gasoline used by U.S. forces and scrap iron were prohibited outside the British Empire and Western Hemisphere, while licenses for other controlled commodities were issued sparingly according to national-defense needs.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal of reply to Congressman Thomas
subfiles.about: Sends Thomas a copy of the Department's response to Rolland Bradley and returns Bradley's letter.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Thomas's referral concerning alleged gasoline shipments to Japan. He encloses the direct response being sent to Bradley and returns the original correspondence.

subfiles.title: Senator Brown forwards Dale O. Miller's export inquiry
subfiles.about: Forwards Miller's letter and enclosure about exports to Japan and requests information for a reply.
subfiles.summary: Brown submits correspondence from Dale O. Miller of Detroit concerning machine tools, oil, and other materials reportedly sold to Japan. He asks that the enclosures be returned with information he can use in answering Miller.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Brown concerning exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Explains U.S. export controls in response to Dale O. Miller's concerns about machine tools, oil, and other shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department cannot verify the particular shipments but notes that the United States had imposed no general embargo on Japan. It describes licensing under the Export Control Act, restrictions on aviation gasoline and scrap iron, and daily adjustment of controls to defense needs. A long list of proclamations, executive orders, regulations, releases, and memoranda is enclosed for Brown's use.

subfiles.title: FBI transmittal concerning licensed Mitsui petroleum shipments
subfiles.about: Forwards an Export Control report identifying petroleum shipments discussed in intercepted or reviewed Mitsui telegrams.
subfiles.summary: Hoover refers to an earlier FBI memorandum quoting telegrams connected with Cities Service and Mitsui in San Francisco. He sends the Export Control Administrator's letter showing that several aviation-gasoline-related shipments had been covered by appropriate licenses and copies naval and military intelligence officials.

subfiles.title: Export Control report on gasoline and lubricating-oil licenses for Japan
subfiles.from: R. L. Maxwell, Administrator of Export Control
subfiles.about: Identifies licenses authorizing several gasoline and lubricating-oil shipments mentioned in Mitsui telegrams.
subfiles.summary: Maxwell details licensed cargoes including 200,000 drums of uncracked gasoline, 3,510,000 gallons of lubricating oil, and smaller quantities of specialized lubricants. He explains why each product fell within current petroleum regulations and states that other proposed shipments were believed to have approved licenses.

subfiles.title: Congressman Ford forwards William B. Murphy's inquiry
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's request for information about shipments of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ford transmits William B. Murphy's letter concerning the volume and character of American exports to Japan. He asks the Department either to answer Murphy directly or supply information that Ford can forward.

subfiles.title: William B. Murphy letter requesting statistics and policy on trade with Japan
subfiles.about: Requests detailed statistics on U.S. exports of iron, steel, oil, gasoline, and cotton to Japan and asks whether policy amounts to appeasement.
subfiles.summary: Murphy acknowledges the diplomatic risk that Japan might move into the South Seas and East Indies but questions the continued flow of potential war materials. He asks for recent and historical figures on quantities, values, and monthly changes and expresses opposition to appeasing authoritarian states.

subfiles.title: Fragment of State Department reply concerning Murphy's export inquiry
subfiles.about: Explains licensing rules applicable to the commodities named in William B. Murphy's letter.
subfiles.summary: The surviving portion states that licenses for controlled exports outside the British Empire and Western Hemisphere were issued sparingly and denied whenever national defense might be harmed. It notes that all commodities Murphy mentioned except cotton were subject to export licensing and lists the governing proclamations, executive orders, regulations, releases, and Division of Controls memoranda.

subfiles.title: Timken inquiry on bearing sales to Russia and Japan
subfiles.about: Requests guidance on whether the Timken Roller Bearing Company should continue accepting Japanese and Soviet orders.
subfiles.summary: Timken explains that bearing shipments to both countries had historically been negligible, though Japanese demand had recently increased as purchases shifted from Germany and Sweden. Because the company's Japanese export operation had largely ceased but outstanding orders remained, it sought the Government's policy before proceeding.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to Timken Roller Bearing Company
subfiles.from: Leonard H. Price for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges information supplied by Timken concerning the firm's sales policies.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that it has noted the information contained in Timken's March 18 communication. It thanks him for informing the Department about the company's policies.

subfiles.title: Senator Maloney forwards Edgar White's complaint about indirect exports
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's concerns about Philippine iron ore going to Japan and American oils and fats reaching Germany through the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Edgar White argues that restrictions on direct American exports are ineffective if the Philippines may ship iron ore to Japan and the Soviet Union may transmit imported fats and oils to Germany. Maloney asks Hull to give the issue immediate and careful consideration.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Maloney on Philippine and Soviet-bound exports
subfiles.about: Clarifies that vegetable oils and fats were not licensed under the cited controls and that the Export Control Act did not govern Philippine exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply distinguishes controlled exports from vegetable oils and fats, which had not been made subject to export licenses. It also explains that the Export Control Act did not apply to shipments from the Philippine Islands to Japan and encloses the principal proclamations, orders, regulations, releases, and memoranda governing export control.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on proposed wording for controlled petroleum products
subfiles.about: Records Walden's suggestion for broadening the proposed definition of petroleum products subject to licensing.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum quotes technical criteria covering aviation motor fuel and high-viscosity petroleum products. Walden suggested replacing “commercial distillation” with “commercial processes” so that the definition would encompass more petroleum products.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Walden and Robinson's views of lubricating-oil controls
subfiles.about: Discusses whether a proposed petroleum definition should include a percentage threshold for recoverable aviation lubricating oil.
subfiles.summary: Walden said Robinson's definition, without a percentage limitation, would cover nearly all lubricating oils, including the product sought by Japanese buyers. Although Walden initially proposed a three-percent threshold using lower viscosity standards, he accepted Robinson's wording. Robinson confirmed that no percentage limitation was intended unless later shown to be desirable.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting large gasoline imports and storage at Qingdao
subfiles.about: Reports the arrival and anticipated delivery of approximately 3.3 million gallons of American gasoline for Mitsubishi and possible further North China purchases.
subfiles.summary: The American steamship Aquarius arrived with 32,084 drums of straight-run motor gasoline from Corpus Christi, and a similar shipment was expected aboard the Scottsburg. The combined volume exceeded the previous year's gasoline sales in Shandong, drums were being moved toward an airfield, and Mitsubishi tanks were associated with a separate inquiry for 300,000 gallons. Meyer also reported a rumor that the China Affairs Board in Tianjin was exploring the purchase of 20 million gallons.

subfiles.title: Duplicate memorandum on Walden and Robinson's views of lubricating-oil controls
subfiles.about: Duplicates the memorandum discussing percentage limits in the proposed definition of licensable lubricating oil.
subfiles.summary: The duplicate records Walden's view that Robinson's definition would cover nearly all lubricating oils, including the product requested by Japanese buyers. It also repeats Robinson's statement that the proposed rule intentionally contained no percentage limitation.

subfiles.title: Senate Committee on Patents referral of L. R. Johnson's letter
subfiles.about: Forwards a Tacoma correspondent's complaint about continued shipments of materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The senator sends Hull a letter received from L. R. Johnson of Tacoma. He asks the Secretary to consider Johnson's concerns about continuing exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Ship Tank Plate to Japan / Seamen Refuse to Carry Japan Gas
subfiles.about: Reports a tank-plate shipment from Tacoma to Japan and a maritime-union crew's refusal to carry gasoline from Houston to Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: The main article says the Florida Maru loaded 450 tons of tank plate at Tacoma, shipped by rail from a tank company in Casper and apparently purchased by C. T. Takahashi & Company. A companion report says 29 National Maritime Union crewmen refused to sign onto the Scottsburg because it carried 75,000 barrels of high-test gasoline to Yokohama. Union official James B. Merrill said the crew opposed sending oil to the Axis powers; the clipping ends mid-report.
